blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 − Q1, the span of the middle 50% of the data. Half of it is the quartile deviation (QD), or semi-interquartile range. The coefficient of quartile deviation is (Q3 − Q1) ÷ (Q3 + Q1), a unit-free version.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The range was ruined by a single extreme value. The IQR discards the lowest and highest quarter of the data and reports the spread of the middle half, the part least affected by extremes.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Five children: IQR = 12 − 10 = 2 kg, against a range of 4 kg.
  2. Today’s 30 children (type 7 quartiles from §3.3): IQR = 13.05 − 10.575 = 2.475 kg; QD = 2.475 ÷ 2 = 1.24 kg; coefficient of QD = 2.475 ÷ (13.05 + 10.575) = 2.475 ÷ 23.625 = 0.105.
  3. Grouped quartiles for the same children: IQR = 13.222 − 10.417 = 2.81 kg; QD = 1.40 kg; coefficient of QD = 2.81 ÷ 23.64 = 0.119. The grouped values differ from the raw ones because grouping spreads values evenly across each class.

points.html: IQR = Q3 − Q1; QD = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ 2; coefficient of QD = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ (Q3 + Q1).
The IQR is the usual companion of the median, as the SD is the companion of the mean (recall §2.5).

Outlier fences (a convention). Values below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR are flagged as possible outliers. This is Tukey’s convention for box-plot whiskers (Tukey, 1977; 1.5 is also the default multiplier in R’s box-plot documentation). NIST calls points beyond these “inner fences” mild outliers and points beyond wider “outer fences” extreme outliers. It is one convention among several: box-plot software may use “hinges” that differ slightly from the quartiles, and a flagged value is a prompt to check, not a licence to delete. For today’s 30 children the fences are 10.575 − 3.71 = 6.86 kg and 13.05 + 3.71 = 16.76 kg, so no child is flagged. Box plots are drawn in §4.3.4.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 3.1

questions.prompt: Two datasets have the same range. Explain how they could still look completely different, and which measure from §3.3–3.4 would catch the difference.
questions.answer: The range uses only the two extremes. One dataset can be tightly clustered with one value at each end (9, 11, 11, 11, 13) while the other is spread evenly (9, 10, 11, 12, 13); both have range 4. The interquartile range, built from the middle 50% of the data, catches the difference: by the type 7 rule the first dataset has Q1 = Q3 = 11 and IQR = 0, and the second has IQR = 12 − 10 = 2.

questions.prompt: A child’s weight is “at the 10th percentile” on a growth chart. Explain what that means without using the word “percentile”.
questions.answer: Among children of the same age and sex in the reference population, 10% weigh less than this child and 90% weigh more. The child is on the light side of the reference, but not extremely so.

questions.prompt: For six women’s haemoglobin values, 9.0, 10.5, 11.0, 11.5, 12.0 and 14.0 g/dL, find Q1 and Q3 by the type 7 rule, the IQR, the quartile deviation and the coefficient of quartile deviation.
